item.title: You May Be the Reason Your Adult Child Can't Move Forward
item.description:
Parenting

You May Be the Reason Your Adult Child Can't Move Forward

Three ways parents keep grown children emotionally stuck. Are you one of them?

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • A diagnosis describes a real limitation. It is not a lifetime waiver from discomfort, effort, or growth.
  • Are you creating dependency or fostering more independence?
  • Guilt wearing support's clothing does not align with helping your adult child move forward.

Every accommodation you make for your adult child is a question in disguise. Yet most parents never stop to ask it. Over my career, I have sat with parents of adult children (and many adult children as well) carrying a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety, depression, or autism. Many adult children struggle who have not been formally diagnosed with a mental health condition. Whatever the causes of the adult child's struggles, many parents are trying to help unhealthily, which is the real reason their adult child can't move forward. It is hard for me to write the previous sentence because I am not about casting blame or judgment when I discuss this painful topic.

It is generally not that the parents don't care. Rather, the parents have become habituated to their adult children's struggles, so they have stopped asking crucial questions. Here are three patterns I see consistently and how to check yourself against them.

1. You Have Let Your Adult Child's Diagnosis Explain Everything

A diagnosis describes a real limitation. It is not a lifetime waiver from discomfort, effort, or growth. When every missed deadline, unpaid bill, canceled plan, or ream-out session at you gets "filed" under "that's just their condition," then you may have stopped distinguishing between what the diagnosis really requires and what has become an excuse. Ask yourself: Is this accommodation I am making appropriate, given what the diagnosis actually requires, or have I quietly expanded its jurisdiction over my adult child's life?

2. You Keep Doing the Work They Need to Learn to Do

This is the one that many of my parent-coaching clients resist seeing most, because it looks like love and care. You make the calls, you pay the overdue bills or parking tickets. Sound familiar? Let's not forget handling their financial affairs entirely or way more than will help them learn to be independent. Perhaps you dramatically edit what you know is best to say—in favor of not ruffling their feathers or hurting their feelings. My question is whether each of these is time-limited or growth-oriented. Are you creating dependency or fostering more independence?

This is precisely why I wrote my latest book, You Ruined My Life, Now You Owe Me! It's about adult children who have learned that their struggles entitle them to a permanent claim on their parents' guilt, time, and money. It is about the parents who have learned that saying "no" is indispensable to avoiding abandonment. The reflective questions may help you begin to look at how your actions are helping your child move forward or contributing to their remaining stuck.

3. You've Let Guilt, Not Judgment, Set the Terms

The most corrosive part of this dynamic with your adult child is not about what you do. It is about who is deciding what you do. If every accommodation you make feels like it is tracing back to "I can't stand feeling like a bad parent," rather than what a professional with this diagnosis would say is helpful, then guilt may be stealing the show. Look, I get that this could be hard for you to admit. Yet please hear that it is all easier to modify if you see your part in the situation more clearly.

The Takeaway

Continue reflecting on the accommodation questions I discussed above. Keep in mind that what survives is healthy support. What does not survive is guilt wearing the support's clothing. Knowing the difference more clearly will likely help your adult child move forward in ways you may not have yet imagined.

item.title: The Transformative Power of Psychological Richness
item.description:
Happiness

The Transformative Power of Psychological Richness

Looking beyond happiness and meaning

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Psychology has focused mainly on two dimensions of a good life: happiness and meaning or purpose.
  • Psychological richness is a new concept of measuring a good life.
  • A psychologically rich life is characterized by curiosity, exploration and experiences that change our views.
  • Psychologically rich moments are those that stretch us, unsettle us, or invite us to see things differently.

For decades, psychologists have focused on two primary pathways to a fulfilled life: happiness and meaning. Happiness emphasizes positive emotions, comfort, and life satisfaction, while meaning centers on purpose, significance, and contribution to something larger than oneself. These two dimensions have dominated research on well-being and shaped much of the public conversation about what it means to live well. Yet, psychologist Dr. Shigehiro Oishi, in his groundbreaking book Life in Three Dimensions: How Curiosity, Exploration, and Experience Make a Fuller, Better Life (2026), introduces a compelling third dimension: psychological richness.

According to Oishi, a psychologically rich life is characterized by curiosity, exploration, novelty, and experiences that change our perspectives. Unlike happiness, which often seeks stability and comfort, or meaning, which seeks purpose and consistency, psychological richness embraces complexity, uncertainty, and growth through new experiences. A psychologically rich life may not always be comfortable, but it is often deeply engaging and memorable.

Oishi argues that happiness and meaning do not fully capture the diversity of human experiences. Many people experience events that challenge their assumptions, broaden their horizons, and reshape how they see themselves and the world. Traveling to unfamiliar places, learning a new language, engaging with different cultures, pursuing creative endeavors, or simply exploring a new perspective can enrich life in ways that go beyond feeling good or fulfilling a purpose. These experiences often leave lasting impressions because they transform us.

A psychologically rich life is not necessarily free of difficulties. In fact, some of the most psychologically enriching experiences involve uncertainty, struggle, or even failure. Moving to a new city, changing careers, experiencing an unexpected event such as a disaster, or stepping outside one’s comfort zone can be stressful, yet these experiences often foster personal growth and expand our understanding of life. Oishi’s research suggests that psychologically rich experiences are marked by novelty and perspective change and the sense that we have seen the world differently because of what we encountered.

This perspective is particularly relevant in today’s rapidly changing world. Modern life often encourages routines, efficiency, and predictability. While these qualities can support happiness and stability, they may inadvertently limit opportunities for exploration and discovery. Many individuals find themselves feeling stuck despite being comfortable and secure. Psychological richness offers an alternative lens through which to evaluate well-being. It asks not only "Am I happy?" or "Does my life have meaning?", but also "Am I growing through new experiences?" and "Am I learning something that changes how I see the world?"

The connection between psychological richness and wellness is especially important. Wellness in today's world extends far beyond physical health. It encompasses emotional, social, cognitive, and spiritual well-being. Curiosity and exploration serve as mechanisms of brain health, keeping the mind active and adaptable. Novel experiences stimulate learning, creativity, and cognitive flexibility. By engaging with diverse perspectives and unfamiliar situations, individuals develop resilience and a greater capacity to navigate life’s complexities. These qualities contribute significantly to overall wellness and health.

Psychological richness also strengthens social well-being. Meaningful interactions often arise when people venture beyond familiar environments and engage with individuals from different backgrounds. Exposure to diverse viewpoints fosters empathy, understanding, and openness. In a world increasingly characterized by social polarization, cultivating curiosity about others can help build stronger connections and reduce barriers between people. Exploration, both physical and intellectual, expands not only what we know but also how we relate to others.

Importantly, pursuing psychological richness does not require dramatic life changes. Oishi emphasizes that enriching experiences can be simple and accessible. Reading books outside one’s usual interests, attending a cultural event, learning a new skill, taking a different route home, or having conversations with people who hold different viewpoints can all contribute to a richer psychological life. The key is openness to novelty and a willingness to embrace experiences that encourage growth and perspective change.

As wellness and mental health professionals, educators, and individuals seek ways to thrive in an increasingly complex world, Oishi’s concept offers a valuable reminder: a good life is not one-size-fits-all. Happiness matters. Meaning matters.

The third is psychological richness, which adds another important dimension. It invites us to approach life with curiosity, courage, and a readiness to explore the unknown. In doing so, we may discover that some of life’s greatest rewards come not from comfort or certainty but from the experiences that surprise us, challenge us, and ultimately transform us.

In today’s world, where wellness is often measured through satisfaction and achievement, psychological richness encourages us to value discovery, wonder, and lifelong learning. By embracing curiosity and exploration, we create lives that are not only happier or more meaningful, but fuller, deeper, and extraordinarily rich.

For those interested in learning more about psychological richness, Dr. Shigehiro Oishi’s interview on Wellness in Today’s World provides a practical and engaging exploration of how psychological richness can be cultivated in everyday life.

item.title: The Changing Face of Autism
item.description:
Autism

The Changing Face of Autism

The autism model you’ve depended on for self-understanding got rescinded.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Two key definitions of autism have been revised by experts.
  • The extreme male brain’ model is now being ‘retired.’
  • Autism as a spectrum is said to be on the point of collapse.
  • Stakeholders in these models are airing their concerns.

Two leading autism experts have significantly revised their highly influential models. Many who are autistic or have some autistic traits, alongside professionals who diagnose ASD or support those with ASD, now confront an upheaval in the framework they have relied on, leaving many feeling confused and unsupported.

Two Models Proposed for the Scrapheap

The first ‘retired’ model of autism: A condition of an ‘extreme male brain’ characterized by being naturally better at systemizing and naturally less good at and less interested in empathizing. The second proposed change is to scrap the long-held position that autism is a spectrum of traits with varying severity and influences.

These significant changes raise several pressing questions for those with ASD or ASD related issues. How do these revisions affect our understanding of autism? Have those who feel part of an autism community been operating with false assumptions?

Questions also arise about the ethical process around highly influential researchers changing, in effect, retracting their views. On the one hand, we should applaud scientists who revise theories in response to new evidence. On the other hand, researchers who have worked hard to promulgate their views, using their professional status as a vehicle for their message, should be responsive to those whose lens of understanding is suddenly shattered. Given how psychological theory has both academic and practical aspects, I propose thinking through guidance in revising, rescinding or ‘retiring’ key influential models.

Why the Extreme Male Brain Is Being ‘Retired’

Following Hans Asperger, who, in 1944, wrote that ‘the autistic personality is an extreme variant of male intelligence,' Simon Baron-Cohen wrote in 2002: The male brain is defined psychometrically as those individuals in whom systemizing is significantly better than empathizing, and the female brain is defined as the opposite cognitive profile. Using these definitions, autism can be considered as an extreme of the normal male profile. [1]

The reasons Simon Baron Cohen now gives for retiring this model are as follows:

  1. The phrase ‘extreme male brain’ ‘lends itself to misunderstanding’ even though ‘the underlying science stood the test of time.’
  2. Language referring to the female brain and the male brain is ‘not useful today.’
  3. Such language can lead to ‘simplistic headlines like “autistic people lack empathy,” which is not true.’
  4. Misunderstanding of the language risks reinforcing gender stereotypes. [2]

These explanations present the proposed changes as minimal, a means of avoiding and correcting common misunderstandings rather than changing the fundamental science. However, to say that it is via ‘misunderstanding’ that this model of autism enforces gender stereotypes, or that it is only via ‘simplistic headlines’ that this models autistic people as lacking empathy is puzzling. It is difficult to see this as anything other than a significant retraction of a position that had been much argued against [3] and much defended by Baron-Cohen.

article continues after advertisement

If the term ‘extreme male brain’ is being ‘retired’ while endorsing the science behind it, then we need some explanation of what ‘science has stood the test of time.’ If that includes key arguments about inborn differences in the intelligence of boys and girls in systemizing (maths, physics, and engineering) versus empathizing (sharing, turn-taking, sensitivity to facial expressions, valuing relationships), then the enforcement of gender stereotypes remains. If this science includes pitting systemizing against empathizing, then empathy still seems out of reach for those with ASD.

Few people regret that the model of autism as ‘an extreme male profile’ is being retired, though some are frustrated that the damage of this influential theory is not acknowledged. For though Baron-Cohen himself, even in the heyday of the popularity of ‘the extreme male brain,’ may himself not have ignored autism in girls or denied that people with ASD feel empathy, his theory did. Asking different questions about autism (for example, how it might be correlated with other medical conditions and what interventions might improve the lives of those with ASD) shifts focus away from a highly problematic model; it does not explain why this model is wrong and what remains correct.

Why Changing the Notion of Autism as a Spectrum Is Proposed

In another disruption to common understandings of autism, Uta Frith argues against the model of autism as a spectrum that is so broad it risks medicalising normal experiences. Her reasons for this proposal are:

  1. The autism spectrum has widened to the ‘point of collapse’ so that a diagnosis itself does not give a picture of key characteristics or point to appropriate support.
  2. An autism diagnosis should be limited to profound autism with cognitive impairment that emerges in early childhood. Later emerging conditions currently described as autism should receive a different diagnosis, such as oversensitivity or anxiety— conditions that call for different resources of support and are capable of very different outcomes. [4]

There have been loud protests against Frith’s revisions from those who feel ASD provides an ‘explanatory and legitimizing framework’ for them and their parents and teachers. But frameworks that feel right are not always scientifically sound, and in my view Frith’s public revision, whether or not we agree, provides an excellent model for the process by which a high-profile expert changes their mind. She shows precisely what changes her revisions require and cites reasons for the suggested changes.

article continues after advertisement

Stakeholders’ concerns about the effects of these changes, that they will lose the definition and gravitas of their current diagnosis, are very different from the scientific reasons for keeping or changing the model. Their concerns warrant engaged discussion about possible benefits and protection from harms resulting from a different diagnosis, but they should not shore up a defective model.

item.title: Six Challenges Later in Addiction Recovery
item.description:
Addiction

Six Challenges Later in Addiction Recovery

There will always be challenges even with the best recovery.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • People in later recovery face different challenges from those early in recovery.
  • Mistaking monotony for boredom may lead to seeking chaos, threatening sobriety.
  • Pride can mask evolving cravings, making them harder to recognize and manage.
  • Rigidly sticking to one recovery method may ignore changing personal needs over time.

There will always be challenges in recovery because challenges are unavoidable facts of life. It doesn’t matter how long someone has been in recovery; there will always be challenges along the way. The challenges later in recovery may differ from those early in recovery.

In the world of addiction treatment, there tends to be more focus on challenges early in recovery. Everything is new, different, and disorienting. It makes a good deal of sense to attend to these challenges because many people early in recovery don’t have their feet under them yet. Relapsing or slipping may be much closer at hand for them.

Later in recovery when people have more experience addressing cravings, navigating tricky social situations, and facing challenges without addictive substances and behaviors, relapsing or having a slip may seem a more distant option.

While a slip or relapse may be more distant and less likely, it isn’t impossible. Here are six challenges that people in long term recovery may experience.


Six Common Challenges in Long-Term Recovery

Complacency: We take our recovery for granted and become more passive towards it. We may act like Julius Caesar who claimed after a quick military victory, “Veni, vidi, vici,” which means “I came, I saw, I conquered.”

The assumption is there won’t be significant challenges at all or any challenges will pale in comparison to having conquered our addictions. If you believe you have already won the biggest battle, you may may be ill-prepared for what may come next.

Monotony: In recovery, our lives are on a more even keel. We may have left the drama cycle of offend, repair, repent, and repeat behind us. There may be a wishfulness for excitement. But we may start to mistake chaos for vibrancy and excitement. When we equate these with fun, we put our sobriety at risk.

Hubris/Pride: It is understandable that we are proud to have worked or lived ourselves into recovery. It requires an enormous amount of effort and dedication. When paired with gratitude and appreciation for how others have helped us on our way and all that recovery has brought us, our pride isn’t troubling.

Our pride becomes dangerous when we begin to tell ourselves that we are not the sort of people who would relapse. Some of us may say, I’ve got too many years under my belt. Others may say, I have put in every fail safe there is because I am always prepared for what may come next. Our pride may lead us to believe that we control far more than we actually do.

Our pride may make it more difficult to recognize how the character of cravings may change the longer we are in recovery. Early in recovery, cravings may feel like a mugger that appears out of nowhere. In long term recovery, the cravings may be more like a long con man.

They may be like the Sirens of Greek mythology who lured sailors to their deaths by singing songs all about the heroic past and future glories of the sailors. Transfixed, the sailors crashed into the shoals and were killed or were shipwrecked but so captivated by the songs they didn’t eat.

Dogmatism/rigidity: A person may begin to tell herself, This program has worked before so it will continue to work. We assume that past performance guarantees future results. Ironically, we may become more committed to a program than we are to our own recovery.

A dogmatic view about what does--and even stronger--must work for us makes it harder to see how much we have changed. As we change in recovery, what we need in recovery may change as well.

Expectations/Desert: Not in dry land sense but in the sense of something that is deserved. We may become so attached to the number of days/months/years sober and how hard we have worked that we start to think that we deserve not to work so hard. We may expect others to constantly validate our choices and behaviors. When they do not adequately do so, we may begin to feel resentment not just towards particular people but to the fact that we had to do this work in the first place.

Faulty vision about the past and about the future: We may begin to rewrite or romanticize using days the longer they are in the rearview mirror. We fail to heed the warning on the side mirror that “objects are closer than they appear.” Even in cars that now beep and buzz when something is in a blind spot, we may begin to ignore it the more often we hear it. We may even turn off that safety feature. With our past use of addictive substances and behaviors, we may reframe them as not all that bad.

When we look to the future, we may assume that having some drinks, placing a few bets, taking a few hits will not negatively affect the present. We put on some rose-tinted glasses as we image a perfect rosy future where we will keep everything we have gained in sobriety while being able to engage in behaviors that in the past came at great cost. We forget that everything is going so much better because we are not using/drinking.

Neither a slip nor relapse is inevitable when people cherish their sobriety. People protect what they cherish when their actions spring from honesty and gratitude, which are cornerstones of recovery.

item.title: Did the Character of You Replace You?
item.description:
Authenticity

Did the Character of You Replace You?

In an on-screen world, life choices are made to create a story of ourselves.

Posted July 15, 2026

Linda was getting married for the second time at age 52. She was remarrying because her to-be-husband’s tax situation was better than her own. This sounded like she should not want to. I asked if she was also excited about marrying Jon; her answer was “not really.” Marriage, as a concept, was something she rejected; she wasn’t one of those trad-wives who drank the Kool-Aid and fell for the cultural narrative. Marriage, she explained, had been created not for love but as an economic arrangement when women were dependent on men and couldn’t work or get an education. The church had romanticized marriage as something sentimental, which the patriarchy was now deliberately using as a form of power and control—to hold women hostage.

We then moved on to a conversation about the wedding day itself. Not surprisingly, Linda wouldn’t buy anything special to wear; she would grab something from her closet that looked clean and casual. The ceremony would take place at City Hall, with random staff serving as their witnesses. Traveling by subway (and only subway), they would meet up for a meal with friends.

To acknowledge that the day might be different or deserve any special attention would indicate that she had been snookered by the patriarchy. She had planned an event to present a woman who wakes up and, on a whim, decides to get married that day—because it’s a fun thing to do and no big deal. All of which makes her someone who breaks the rules—but always in just the right ways.

The purpose of the wedding day then shifted and was a way to create a different character. In this case, Linda wanted to be viewed as someone “important,” relevant on a societal level. To project that character, and support that story of herself, City Hall would be followed by the hottest restaurant in the city, and the hardest place to get a reservation. The paradox of the everyday subway next to the exclusivity of the dining spot was not random and had also been carefully curated.

“Is that a cuisine you particularly enjoy?” I asked because the restaurant was known for its eclectic and limited menu. “Not particularly,” she said, “I don’t really like eating out, and if I do, it's at a diner. And I never stay up past 9:30 anyway."

As for the post-party, she'd "planned" it at a private club, one that was apparently too exclusive to have a phone number, which made it impossible to confirm that it would happen. But no matter how stressful, Linda persevered with her plan. It wasn’t a day to enjoy; her wedding experience wasn’t even on the radar. Rather, it was an event to be remembered as the hippest event of the year, and her as the hippest host. Hers would be the invitation you wanted—a true insider’s event. She wanted the character of Linda to be known as someone who was all that.

The problem was this: Linda didn’t want to do any of it. No part of the day sounded enjoyable—for her. Her wedding was an event she didn’t want to attend. Designed for her use—as a means to assert a certain identity. This cool, important, smart, and savvy character, who would be “posted” everywhere, would then serve as a stand-in for her.

Bringing the conversation back to something more authentic, I asked Linda, “Why do you want to marry this particular man, of all the men on earth?” Linda had a beautiful answer that made her smile. “He will always be my favorite person to talk to,” she said. It was the first moment when I felt Linda in the room with me, as if she had suddenly poured herself into herself, and her heart had connected with her head. Her mental narratives dropped away, and we were in conversation with something real.

And so I asked: If you were to design a day you would actually look forward to (not dread), one that you’d be happy living, what would it contain and which people and or pets would you want with you? What I wanted to know was what made a day a good day, a nourishing day—for her? What made her smile effortlessly, without her mind’s help?

Linda recognized that the day she’d planned did not bring her joy or connect her with her love and appreciation for her partner. Furthermore, how infrequently she even thought about her own joy. Her wedding day had been kidnapped by her story of marriage and her own story of herself. But this is where it got fun, as she set out to discover and design an experience that she actually wanted to attend.

In the age of technology, when everyone is living on screen, we've shifted from a first-person experience of ourselves to a third-person perspective. How we're choosing to live is being determined more and more by the perception we imagine we will create through our choices. Simply put, we do what we do because of what we think it will say about us. The problem is, we’ve stopped living our lives from the inside, seeing our lives as something that should matter to us and bring us joy. The character we've constructed has become more important than who we actually are, and what our choices say about us is more important than the experience of living out those choices.

What wags your tail? What makes a day a good day? Imagine if you were to live your life from the inside out, to let what you genuinely feel guide your choices. What if the goal of life weren’t just to die with a well-curated identity, having created a successful character, a story that worked? What if there were more to life than successfully maintaining the project you call “me”?

item.title: What Organizational Psychology Teaches Us About Parenting
item.description:
Parenting

What Organizational Psychology Teaches Us About Parenting

Your organization is not your family, but your family is an organization.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Industrial/organizational psychology considers how best to provide support within organizational parameters.
  • We must know how bias and heuristics affect decision-making, how people learn, and what motivates performance.
  • We must listen in order to develop our families, as much to earn collective buy-in and surface new insights.

“This organization is like a family” is among the most hypocritical statements in the corporate lexicon. Unless, of course, your family lets go of underperformers.

But while an organization is not your family, your family is an organization. So, what can be gleaned from the traditional pillars of the field? Quite a lot, actually.

Selection

Industrial and organizational (I/O) psychology teaches that a) structured interviews improve hiring decisions by up to 300 percent by countering bias,1 and b) no one ever does structured interviews, because we prefer relying on gut instincts over a laborious process, regardless of efficacy.

This is driven by biases and heuristics, which exist to save our mental energy. And while they work in some contexts, they consistently fail in others. Like hiring. More than 50 percent of hiring decisions fail.2

Here’s what that means at home. Without a process, decisions make us. And they seek to minimize effort, which usually means accommodating the most difficult family member.

This hits every household decision: activities, friends, meals, routines, rules, media, priorities, and generally, “the way things get done around here” (Deal & Kennedy describing organizational culture).

Like structured interviews, steps can be taken at home to prevent bias from overtaking decision-making. For family activities, rotate decision-making or offer options and vote. If you want your kid to take piano lessons, make sure they get to choose an equivalent activity to balance out the decision-making. Or, you can use counter-programming questions before deciding. “What theoretical evidence would suggest we should not make this decision?”

Training

Training begins with motivation. If our kids don’t want to learn something, that’s the problem to solve. Since the only way to change an attitude is to change a belief, we have to find ways to convey to our children why it matters.

Next comes cognitive load. Human beings can hold about four concepts in working memory,3 and most training programs blow past that in the first five minutes. If we want training to be effective, we must make it short and frequent, because that’s how the brain works.

The next consideration is training transfer. We can’t just “teach” our kids. We have to create space and support for them to practice.

And the classic instructional design acronym “A.D.D.I.E.” works perfectly in our homes: assess the need, design the learning, develop the content, implement the teaching, and evaluate the effectiveness.

Performance Management

There are two primary reasons that corporate performance management is so widely considered ineffective. Firstly, organizations try to accomplish two things simultaneously that fundamentally undermine each other: evaluation and motivation. It’s like trying to be a referee and a coach at the same time.

Secondly, managers have no incentive to provide honest feedback. Lives are much simpler when telling everyone, “Good job,” than when identifying problems for which they themselves will be held accountable to solve.

The best performance management approaches separate evaluation and motivation into discrete initiatives. The first is for management to understand its talent, and the second is to get the best performance from the team. They provide clear expectations of evaluative criteria. And they compare people to their past selves rather than to others. Parents should do all three.

Leadership

Procedural organizational justice says you must treat everyone the same. Situational leadership theory says you must treat everyone differently. How can both be valid? Context.

There are very few hard-and-fast leadership rules that apply in every situation, but there are themes. Transformational leadership shows that inspiring people generally works better than transacting with them (“Do this to keep your job”). Servant leadership demonstrates that a focus on the long-term well-being of followers generally leads to better performance. And we know that referent power (respect, affection, loyalty) generally triggers stronger intrinsic motivation, whereas the opposite is true for positional power.

As parents, our best focus is on inspiring our kids, not directing them. On demonstrating how our decisions are being made with their long-term interests in mind. And on knowing that they are more likely to follow our lead because of good feelings than “Because I said so.”

Motivation

The relevance of motivation science for parenting could fill a book, so here are some of the greatest hits.

Incentives gone wrong are an irresistible subject for many, yet we rarely stop to consider the incentives we provide our children. Do we pay more attention to them when they misbehave? Then we are incentivizing them to misbehave.

Expectancy theory identifies three prerequisites to motivation: A) the person believes they can do it, B) the person wants the reward, and C) the person believes they’ll actually get the reward. Managers, like parents, usually assume all three, a costly mistake in both instances.

Self-determination theory says three fundamental needs create intrinsic motivation: autonomy, mastery, and connection. For parents, that means letting our kids figure out for themselves how to accomplish their goals on their own, creating opportunities and recognition for demonstrating talent, and making sure they feel a strong sense of connection with us and our communities.

Organizational Development

Successful organizational development strategies keep two fundamental ideas perpetually top of mind. Firstly, change is constant. Secondly, you have to listen to know what to do.

Here’s something non-obvious about organizational listening: interviews, focus groups, surveys, or 360s. They also communicate: “If we’re asking about this, you know it’s important.”

As parents, we can’t just jump in with our own ideas on how to develop the family. We have to listen first, as much to surface insight as to generate buy-in and to convey priorities.

And since every home needs a good model for change, let’s use Kurt Lewin’s, who said change happens in three stages symbolized by water. Stage 1 is unfreezing the ice. Stage 2 is reshaping the water. Stage 3 is refreezing ice in a new shape.

The reason why most organizational efforts fail4 is that they skip Stage 1 and begin at Stage 2. Until people are unfrozen, however, change simply is not possible. With change, we must undo before we can do. The same is true for our families.

Much of I/O psychology exists to mitigate our worst tendencies. Seems like a pretty worthwhile goal for home, too.
